title: Pauri 16, sound: panch parvaan
tomorrow: Pauri 16, meaning: the bull is dharma

cards: For eight stanzas, Japji has been a drumbeat of one word: suniai, suniai, suniai, then mannai, mannai, mannai. Short lines, the same opening every time. Now the music changes.
Pauri 16 is longer, wider, and it opens with a line you can almost clap to: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan. Two halves, like two footsteps.
After this, the stanzas start counting the uncountable: worlds, devotions, fools, names. But first, just the sound of the door into it.

teach.b: Here is the opening line in the original: panch parvaan panch pardhaan. Four words, and two of them the same. Panch, said PUNCH, is the key word.
It can mean five, and it also means the chosen ones, the respected ones, the way a village council in Punjab was called a panchayat.
Here commentators read it as the chosen ones, though some keep the five: people who have listened and trusted, the ones the last eight stanzas were describing. More on that tomorrow.
Parvaan, par-VAAN: accepted, approved, the way a coin is accepted as genuine.
Pardhaan, par-DHAAN: foremost, the chief, the same word Punjabis still use for the president of a committee. So: the chosen are accepted; the chosen are foremost.

The next three lines, in paraphrase: the chosen receive honor in the Court of God; the chosen shine even at the doors of kings; the chosen keep their attention on the one Guru. Listen to how the line is built.
Panch opens both halves, like a bell struck twice.
Parvaan and pardhaan rhyme, both ending on the long aan. That's why it's easy to say and hard to forget. From here the stanza stretches out, to a bull holding up the earth and countless worlds.
That's tomorrow. Today, just get the first line into your mouth.

how: Pauri 16 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning by many Sikhs; its opening line, panch parvaan panch pardhaan, marks the turn from the listening and trusting stanzas to the longer stanzas on creation's countlessness.

o: a village council of five elders

games.q: the sound of Pauri 16 — tap the pairs.

games.q: you hear panch parvaan, panch pardhaan for the first time. who are the panch, as commentators read it?
o: the chosen ones, who have listened and trusted.
games.why: commentators read panch as the chosen ones, the people the listening and trusting stanzas described; they are accepted and foremost.

practice: Say the first line aloud, slowly, feeling each syllable: panch parvaan, panch pardhaan.
Say it three or four times, letting the two halves fall like footsteps, then let the words go quiet and sit with the rhythm still moving in you. If a thought comes, let panch parvaan bring you back.

wordCard.voice: Pardhaan. Foremost, the chief: what the chosen are, panch pardhaan, alongside panch parvaan, accepted.
